speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EDUCATION CONFERENCE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF MEETING IN INDIA
speechtext:
I wish to inform the house that at the invitation of the government of India the second commonwealth education conference will be held in New Delhi from January 11 to January 25, 1962. An announcement to this effect is being made today in the various commonwealth capitals and by the commonwealth education liaison committee in London, which is responsible for the co-ordination of the commonwealth education program.
Canada will, of course, accept the invitation of the government of India to attend the conference, and in due course the government will announce the composition of a representative delegation competent to contribute in a constructive manner to the success of the conference.
It will be recalled that the first commonwealth education conference was convened at Oxford, England, in July, 1959 following an initiative taken by Canada at the conference of commonwealth finance ministers in Montreal in September, 1958. The Oxford conference recommended that a second meeting should be held after an appropriate interval to examine in retrospect the general progress of the program and, in the light of experience gained in the first few years of its operation, to consider in what manner the arrangements for co-operation among the countries of the commonwealth could be improved.
The commonwealth scholarship and fellowship plan, which came into effective operation with the beginning of the scholastic year in September, 1960, has already made substantial progress toward its goal of having 1,000 students studying in various commonwealth countries at any one time, at an intake rate of 500 students per year; and it is expected that by the end of 1961 almost all commonwealth countries will have made or offered awards under the plan.
For the first year of the plan's operation 338 scholarships and three fellowships were awarded by all participating countries; of 90205-6-374i
these, 281 scholarships and the three fellowships were in fact accepted. I am happy to be able to report that, in that period, from the total of 281 scholarships we in Canada have had the pleasure of receiving as our guests 101 commonwealth scholars from 25 different countries or areas of the commonwealth. I might add that they are very widely distributed, as follows: Australia, 9; Basutoland, 1; Bermuda, 1; British Guiana, 2; British Honduras, 1; Ceylon, 5; Fiji, 1; Ghana, 5; India, 14; Kenya, 3; Malaya, 2; Malta, 2; Mauritius, 2; New Zealand, 4; Nigeria, 2; Pakistan, 8; Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, 4; Sierra Leone, 1; Somaliland, 1; South Africa, 4; Tanganyika, 1; Uganda, 4; United Kingdom, 13; Singapore, 2; and the West Indies, 9. This autumn we shall be receiving approximately 115 additional commonwealth scholars, so that by the second year of the scheme's operation Canada will have well over 200 of these welcome visitors from across the seas.
The scholars from abroad have done very well in their studies in Canada, which is a tribute to the care exercised by the special nominating committees in their own countries and in Canada by a scholarship selection committee set up for this purpose. The Canadian universities which received the commonwealth scholars deserve a great deal of credit for their successful efforts.
In addition to the Canadian scholarship and fellowship program, significant advances have been made in the area of training and supplying teachers. Although the United Kingdom has carried the largest share of the responsibility in this particular respect, Canada has assisted both by sending teacher trainers to help in the development of teacher training institutions in other commonwealth countries and by receiving trainees to undertake teacher training courses in Canada. Arrangements also exist whereby Canada and other commonwealth countries which have the necessary facilities available send selected teachers and advisers from their own education services to fill key posts in countries where they are most required. By the end of 1960 Canada had sent abroad a total of 20 educators to assist in teaching and teacher training, and plans for significant expansion in this particular field of activity are well under way.
Another important area of co-operation in commonwealth education is that of technical

Wheat Sales to Poland education, where existing plans are being developed and expanded in accordance with the recommendations of the Oxford conference.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I saw the report in this morning's press of the statements attributed to the Japanese ambassador in a speech made, I believe, in Regina yesterday. Some of these statements are, to say the least, somewhat surprising. The export restraints which the Japanese government is applying on certain exports to Canada in the year 1961 were set forth in a letter written to me by the Japanese ambassador and tabled by me in the house some weeks ago.
These restraints were accepted by the Japanese government, and the kind of statement attributed to the Japanese ambassador in the morning's press it seems to me, is not in harmony or in tone with the letter written to me in setting forth those restraints which the Japanese government is voluntarily applying in 1961 on these designated commodities. These decisions of the Japanese government, as the letter itself indicated, were arrived at by decision of the Japanese government and I think that is perfectly clear.
The whole problem here, as all hon. members are aware, is the degree of concentration of Japanese exports in certain commodities. The Canadian government at all times has indicated its belief that trade between these two countries must be on a two way basis. We look forward to the expansion of trade between the two countries, but not on the basis of continued concentration of Japanese exports in certain selected commodities. That is the position we have taken consistently. We welcome the expansion of trade between the two countries, but not when it takes the form of this concentration to the point where the conditions of competition which Canadian producers are called upon to meet are, in the view of most Canadians, not fair.

speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. C-92, to amend the Criminal Code (capital murder). (Translation):

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of speaking at length at this stage, but after the bill has been considered by the committee of the whole, I should like to make a few brief remarks.
This bill does not amend the definition of murder as found in sections 201 and 202 of the Criminal Code, but it divides it into two classes, capital and non-capital, according as the crime is planned and deliberate or not.
On second reading, I suggested that this definition, along with other provisions of this bill, constitutes in practice, if not in principle, 

an almost complete suppression of capital punishment. Besides, the remarks made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on May 29 last, leave no doubt on that score. In fact, I shall now quote a few lines from the speech of the Prime Minister, as reported on page 5527 of Hansard. This is what he said then:
(Text):
I feel that responsibility for carrying out the law and maintaining the safety of the public in each area depends on the jury. Having heard the evidence and having come to the conclusion on the basis of the law as explained to them by the judge that a verdict of guilty is the only one they can bring in, a jury ought none the less to have the right to add a recommendation to mercy, and having done that, to hope that the royal prerogative will be reasonably carried out.
The Prime Minister went on to say further, and I quote from page 5528 of Hansard of May 29:
Responsibility now rests squarely upon the jury to determine in its area and on the particular facts of each case what is just and fair, what constitutes the proper course to be followed in the opinion of those who have heard all the evidence and live in the community in which they are desirous of maintaining justice and equity as between the crown and the subject.
These remarks and, indeed, the whole speech made by the Prime Minister leave no room for any other interpretation. I wish also to quote from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of May 30, 1961, the first paragraph of which states:
Prime Minister John Diefenbaker indicated clearly today that recommendations for mercy by juries on behalf of murderers sentenced to death will almost always be accepted by the government.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I also want to read into the record the first paragraph of an article which appeared in the L'Action Catholique of Tuesday, May 30, under the following title:
The cabinet and the recommendations by the jury.
And I quote:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker stated yesterday that the federal cabinet would have to accept recommendations for clemency by the juries in murder cases.
Moreover, said the head of the government, the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General should be the only two people deciding whether a sentence should be commuted, and not the cabinet as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, when the matter was discussed in the committee of the whole, all hon. members tried, I think, to make this bill as practical and efficient as possible, while taking into consideration the upsurge in the incidence of crime in this country, and throughout North America.
I should point out that, following our studies and discussions on clause 1 and the resulting suggestions, significant amendments were

submitted, several of which were accepted by the government, at the request of members of the official opposition, among whom the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh).
While discussing clause 2 we moved various amendments which the government thought it could not accept. Yet the fact of those amendments having been submitted indicates that the bill should be reconsidered so as to meet public opinion with regard to the death penalty.
Moreover, during the discussion of clause 13, we tried to convey to the government that this clause, in particular, was entirely devoid of practical sense.
We moved an amendment which was rejected. And I very respectfully submit that this clause introduces an innovation in our statutes. Hon. members are very much concerned with regard to that clause being passed. I, for my part, cannot accept it, because I think it absolutely impracticable; it will indeed put the jurors in an extremely awkward position and the judges in an impossible one.
I repeat what I said yesterday: when it is proved that a capital crime was committed, when the jury assumes its responsibilities in recognizing the accused guilty of the crime and at the same time decides to make a. recommendation for mercy, the judge is placed in the ridiculous position of having to sentence the accused to death, whereas we know very well that, in most cases, the cabinet has the moral obligation of carrying out the jury's recommendation for clemency.
I therefore think that this clause should be reconsidered because it is lacking in realism and we have not every day the opportunity of discussing such a significant bill. Moreover, the minister knows, and the government should realize, that we are introducing new legislation in regard to such an exceptional and important issue as the death penalty.
Let us therefore make sure that any amendments we pass with regard to our statutes are of a practical nature.
Mr. Speaker, the bill has certainly been improved following discussion in the committee of the whole, but it has not yet been tested by experts in criminal law and I would remind the Minister of Justice that when, in the United Kingdom, it was thought proper to amend the law with regard to the death penalty, it was done with the greatest of care. Amendments were introduced only after thorough and searching studies had been completed by experts.
As the minister is aware, the Gower commission was established in 1949, its final re-
Criminal Code
port was submitted in 1953 and it is only in 1957, after further studies, that the 1957 homicide act was passed by parliament in London.
In this country, the government has introduced this bill which, as I have already said, is not based on conclusions arrived at by a committee of experts. I do not question the knowledge of the Minister of Justice and his advisers in this matter, but, with all due respect, I must say that these advisers seem to be lacking that direct court experience which would enable them to express an opinion on the major clauses which represent a new law and to tell us whether these clauses would have any practical value before a court under existing procedures.
Mr. Speaker, for these reasons, I submit that the bill should be given further consideration and, supported by the hon. member for Megantic-
(Text):
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge):
That Bill No. C-92 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred to a special committee for the purpose of further study and examination and that such selected committee shall have the power to send for persons, papers, and things.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support the amendment just put forward by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschate-lets) on third reading of this bill.
I should like to make a few general remarks to explain why I support the amendment.
On second reading, according to Hansard, at least 30 hon. members spoke in the debate, including the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), thus enabling us all to benefit from their experience.
When the bill was considered by the committee of the whole, many hon. members commented on practically every single clause. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) deemed it fitting, following the speech of the leader of the official apposition (Mr. Pearson) to refer to his own experience.
Personally, on section 1, I twice urged the minister and the government to allow the bill to be referred to a special committee, which could hear experts on criminal law, people who have practised in criminal courts.
I now paraphrase what I had to say at the time: We are here as a group of legislators, and I think we should use every means provided by parliamentary procedure to gain more information on this proposal.

Division
When the bill was considered in committee, a number of amendments were put forward, even by members on the government side. I refer particularly to the member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) who suggested an amendment to section 2.
The amendments to section 1, both in the English and French versions, were accepted by the government.
At least two amendments were put forward concerning clause 2 and another one concerning clause 13.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the proposed amendments indicate that there is still some doubt in the minds of hon. members and it would be advisable, I think, that this bill in its present form be referred to a special committee of this house.
One of the main objections of the minister against referring this bill to a committee of this house is that such procedure would delay the adoption of the bill. It is true that such procedure would cause some delay.
However, I do not believe that any prejudice would result for those who are to be judged under the present Criminal Code.
Indeed, the experience of these last three years indicates that the government or the governor general in council, exercising the royal prerogative has commuted, I think, some 40 death penalties to life imprisonment.
If while the bill is being studied by a special committee any case arose under the Criminal Code, nothing would prevent the governor general in council from exercising the royal prerogative once again.
For all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I support the motion put forward by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost. The question is on the main motion. (Translation):

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even though the bill was considerably improved due to the suggestions of the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) which were accepted by the minister, I feel that it could certainly stand further improvement so as to be acceptable to those who are against the abolition or reduction of punishment in capital cases. And I am entirely opposed to the abolition of capital punishment. As I said on second reading, where the issue was the principle of the bill, I feel that clause 13 which puts the jury in an extremely difficult situation is a clause which in my opinion tends to cover the minister who seems inclined to abolish capital punishment indirectly.
I suggest that it would be very difficult under such a procedure to find a jury who, faced by the accused, the defence counsel, a family in tears, would be ready to answer: "No", when the judge would put the question:	"Are you prepared to recommend
mercy?" Moreover, as the Prime Minister said, we know that it would be necessary and practically justifiable for the cabinet to take into account the recommendation for mercy when taking a decision.
Consequently, this is an indirect and practically inevitable way of abolishing capital punishment. Now, I feel we should maintain capital punishment. In my opinion, if the cabinet wanted to abolish it, they should have had the courage of saying plainly: "We want capital punishment to be abolished." Then, at least, we would have known what was the cabinet's position on that question. Under this bill which may otherwise contain very good sections, people who do not have the proper legal training to pass on this matter, will be forced to give the government an indirect means of abolishing capital punishment. If the minister had really wanted to be of service, if he had really wanted to improve his bill, he could have accepted the suggestion which was made to him, namely to compel the judge to say to the jury before they file out to deliberate: "You have the right to recommend or not to recommend mercy for the accused." But that would not have been said in front of the people who usually attend a murder trial, those people who are curious to see how the trial will turn out. The jury would thus have been able to deliberate freely in its private quarters without being influenced by the people around them; we would then have been able to say that the jury's recommendation was based on facts, on a thorough examination, that it has not been brought about
Division
by the embarrassment caused to them by the judge asking that question in the presence of the audience.
Because of that and because of the fact that, in my opinion, too much consideration is being shown to a handful of criminals at the expense of the vast number of honest people whom we must protect, I will vote against the bill.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again while the house has been in session one of our members has passed away. This morning he

was about ready to attend the session when he became suddenly ill. He was taken to hospital, where he passed away.
I refer, of course, to William Anderson, a deeply beloved member of this house. He served in the city council of Galt for a period of 12 years before becoming mayor, a position which he occupied for three years. I do not know anyone of whom it could be said in a truer sense than our late friend, that amid all the vicissitudes and thrusts of parliament he enjoyed to a great extent the affection of members in all parts of the house.
Many there are who know of the work he did in helping others. I think of his work in connection with the Red Cross, the contributions as blood donor that he made to that institution, unostentatiously and as silently as he did many other kind deeds. In other fields of endeavour, too, it can be said of him that he loved to serve others. He was on three committees of the house, research, estimates and miscellaneous private bills. He gave devotedly of his best to the service of his constituents, his province and his country. To his widow, his daughter Jean Elizabeth and his son Donald William I express a deep sense of personal sorrow at his passing.
After hon. gentlemen opposite have paid their tributes I intend to suggest, if the house is agreeable, that we adjourn this afternoon until 7.30 this evening. By our adjournment we will reveal in a tangible way something of the feelings that are ours and at the same time we do that which he would have expected us to do, namely carry on our responsibilities.
Again, sir, through you, I extend the sympathy not only of ladies and gentlemen on this side of the house but I know of all sections of this chamber.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the passing of Mr. William Anderson the House of Commons mourns yet another of its members who had contributed in more ways than one to the public life of his country. He was the mayor of his city, the representative of a constituency that was highly industrialized, which he represented in this house not only with competence but certainly with faithfulness and loyalty to his constituents.
It is not always easy, sir, to represent a constituency such as that which the hon. member served so faithfully and well from the time he was elected. We on this side of the house feel particularly for the Prime Minister and the members of his party on this occasion. We have been told that not only did this member work hard but that he had driven the whole of last evening and into the night on his way back to perform his duties in the house. There is no doubt that this,
The Late W. Anderson along with the other many duties that he performed in the house and elsewhere, took a toll on his physical capacities. There is also the fact that here goes another young man, because relatively speaking he was still a man of youthful age and one who would unquestionably have performed many more tasks for his country.
We join with you, sir, in expressing to your party our deep condolences. To his bereaved widow and his two children go our profound sympathy.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, members of this group join with the Prime Minister, the hon. member for Laurier and all members of the house in expressing our sincere sympathy for this sad and unexpected event. I must say on this sad and in this case quite unexpected occasion words are completely inadequate to express the deep feelings of us all. All in this group extend to his widow and children our most sincere sympathy and trust, Mr. Speaker, that they will find some comfort in the knowledge that he will be long remembered by many people as a colleague, as a friend, as a neighbour and as one given to good works for others and his community.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
Perhaps in this sad moment I might be permitted to say a word. I suppose I knew the late William Anderson perhaps longer than any member of the house. We were natives of the city of Galt. He had been a student of my father at the Galt Collegiate Institute years ago, and there was a very warm bond of friendship between his family and mine and between him and me personally.
I think we are all numbed by the shock of this sad news that has come to us. The hand of death has been laid upon him with great suddenness and with no warning.
On an occasion of this kind, Mr. Speaker, I know it is superfluous to attempt to convey those deepest feelings that such an experience stirs; but I think it can be said of William Anderson that he had won the wholesome regard and complete respect of all members of the house, just as in his own community he enjoyed the widest measure of respect and regard. He had won these rewards by his own native qualities. He was a completely unselfish man. He was unassuming. He had a great desire to be of service to others. This characterized not only the service that he rendered in the municipal sphere and in parliament but all his contacts with other people. There are many people who will be able to testify to a host of personal kindnesses rendered to them and to others within their knowledge by the late William Anderson, a
5932	HOUSE OF
The Late W. Anderson kindly man to the roots of his being. We mourn the passing of one of God's gentlemen.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might be permitted to take a few minutes to say a few words about the late Bill Anderson, whom it was my pleasure to know most intimately for some years. Our ridings adjoin one another. During our last session we roomed together, and I got to know Bill possibly better than others may have. I always found him a most beloved and respected friend, and I am sure I speak for all those in the house when I say just that.
Bill was very well known in his area of Galt and Waterloo South. He rendered great service to that community. He was most interested in the work with retarded children, so much so that the first school in Canada for retarded children was built in Galt. That school bears the name, "The William Anderson School for Retarded Children", and it will be there for years to come as a tribute to the memory of this great and noble public servant.
I should like at this time to express my feelings of sorrow to his wife Jean, his daughter Betty and his son Don, and I can do no better than to use the words of the author who once said, "The light he leaves behind shines upon the path of men".

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to place on the record some remarks made by our beloved friend, William Anderson, in the restaurant only this morning. He left his home at eleven o'clock last night and arrived in Ottawa at five o'clock this morning, and in the restaurant he said he had driven all night in order that he might be here for the opening of today's session. He mentioned that he had only missed four of the 58 votes that have been taken in the house, and I am sure we shall all say that this is an amazing record of faithful service.
I knew Bill Anderson well because he occupied the room in this building next to mine and our relationships were always excellent. He often came into my room to tell a story, and his stories were always appropriate and fitted the point he was trying to make. The devotion to duty and hard work of Bill Anderson for the constituency he represented are undoubtedly responsible for his passing today. Bill Anderson died because he used a drug, and the drug he used was hard work. To his widow and his children whom he has left behind go my deepest and most sincere sympathy.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every member of the house has reason to feel a deep personal loss in the


passing of the hon. member for Waterloo South. As his seatmate during the twenty-third parliament and during the first three sessions of the current parliament, I feel I must add my words to those that have already been spoken. I know that every member of the house without exception will long remember Bill Anderson.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution provides for the appointment of one judge to the Exchequer Court of Canada, of one judge to the court of appeal for British Columbia, of two county court judges for Ontario, of one district court judge for Alberta and of two puisne judges to the superior court of Quebec.
I should like to deal only with the appointment the minister intends to make to the superior court of Quebec. Last year, the minister introduced legislation in the house to amend the Judges Act. At that time, the province of Quebec requested six judges. However, the minister saw fit then to appoint only four, one for the district of Three Rivers, and three for the district of Montreal. In addition, when he was asked why he was not appointing six judges immediately, he stated then, as reported in Hansard for June, 21, 1960, that under an agreement with the Quebec administration of the day, he had been told, and I quote:
-they have agreed that the provision of three extra judges at this time, as soon as we can do it, will be a real contribution toward meeting that need. Therefore, there is no quarrel between us on this point.
Later on, while the bill was given first reading, the minister said that, although he was no expert, he felt he had grounds for appointing only three judges for
Judges Act
the time being. He added that the matter had been discussed with the former government and that three judges were sufficient at the moment.
It is a fact, however, that the Montreal district has a tremendous backlog of cases, and that the appointment of additional judges would permit disposing of them. The minister added that a committee would be set up to revise the code of civil procedure and that any resulting amendments would facilitate the introduction of cases and consequently would speed up the hearing of trials. Perhaps I may travel from west to east, as it were, in replying to the various comments which have been made. The hon. member for Kootenay West asked

Judges Act
me on what basis I arrived at a decision to ask parliament to provide an extra salary for an additional judge of the court of appeal of British Columbia. As long ago as 1956, I think, the legislature of British Columbia passed legislation providing for the appointment of additional judges to the court of appeal of that province. When we took office in 1957 I discussed the question with the attorney general and with the chief justice of the court and was advised that there was no pressing need for an appointment to be made then. From time to time since then I have noted that the court of appeal has got behind in its work. Then it caught up again, and the pressure of the work grew once more. I have been keeping a close watch on the situation because in recent months the work of the court of appeal has increased considerably in British Columbia and it is a fact that they are behind in their lists.
In addition it must be borne in mind that last year by an amendment to the appropriate act we provided that the judges of the court of appeal of British Columbia will be judges of the court of appeal of the Yukon. Previously the court of appeal of British Columbia was the court of appeal of the Yukon. Litigants from the Yukon had to travel south to Vancouver or Victoria to have their appeals heard. Now we have constituted a court of appeal for the Yukon itself and a judge from the court of appeal from British Columbia goes to the Yukon territory and, together with other judges, forms the court of appeal in that territory. This means that from time to time a judge of the court of appeal of British Columbia will be out of the province. For this reason, plus the normal increase in litigation, plus the desire of the court to sit at all times in two banks it has seemed appropriate now to allow for a salary to provide for the appointment of an extra judge.
No one here has raised a question in connection with Alberta for which province we are asking a salary for an additional district court judge. However, I can assure hon. members of the committee that I have heard from the attorney general and from the chief judge of the northern judicial district and am satisfied there is good reason for asking provision for this additional appointment.
With respect to Ontario we are asking for provision of salaries for two additional county court judges. I have heard from the attorney general of Ontario by letter and I have also had discussions with him and I am satisfied that there is a present need for two additional judges of the county court. I am sure hon. members will appreciate that in the province of Ontario, widespread as it is, with many counties and districts served by county and district court judges, a situation frequently

prevails when a judge in one district falls ill and is unable to discharge his duties. This means that judges from another district have to be sent in and that district, in turn, is left short of judges to serve it. An experiment has been tried recently under the authority of legislation in Ontario of appointing a judge at large, a judge to serve all the districts and counties of Ontario. Judge Wilmott is a judge who is doing that work now and I am informed that this is a signal service to the county and district courts of Ontario. This enables counties which would otherwise be very much behind with the work to receive services they would otherwise not receive.
The request I have received from the attorney general of Ontario is that, if this parliament should authorize salaries to pay two additional district court judges, they would be appointed to the district courts of Ontario.
With respect to the province of Quebec, the hon. member for Papineau reminded us of the discussion last week during which time the government of that province had provided for the positions of five extra judges of the superior court in the Montreal district. We appointed three at that time for reasons which I gave, and which my hon. friend summarized. I suggested that we would keep up with the situation in order to see whether the appointment of these three judges was sufficient to make reasonable progress in reducing the backlog of cases. I am informed by the chief justice that the backlog is as serious as ever. It seems, therefore, to be appropriate now to make provisions for the salaries allowing the appointment of two more judges.
I am fully aware of the accommodation problem in the Montreal courthouse, and can only remind my hon. friend that this is a problem for the provincial government. That government is responsible for providing courthouse facilities where the judges who hold court will sit. My understanding is that a statement has been made that a new courthouse will be provided in Montreal. It does seem to me, therefore, appropriate at this time to provide salaries for the paying of two extra judges. If in fact there is no physical accommodation for them provided, we do not need to appoint them. However, at the first moment accommodation is made available they could be appointed, but to do so we will have to provide for the payment of their salaries, and it seems appropriate to do so at this time. I do not suggest that one or the other could physically be accommodated at this time because judges are very often away from their home districts on other duties. However, I am fully aware of and in agreement with the suggestion made by my hon. friend that physical facilities which exist at

this time are far from adequate. I repeat, I do feel that provision should be made now so that the appointments can be made at the first appropriate and convenient time.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Fullon thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-104, to amend the Judges Act and the Exchequer Court Act.

The provisions of section 33 were taken almost textually from the Food and Drugs Act, but at that time possession constituted an offence under that act. We live in a country which follows the principle that the accused does not necessarily have to step into the box to offer a defence until a case has been made against him. I now invite the minister's attention to subsection 3 of section 33, which reads:

Subsection 3 of section 33 definitely indicates that the accused shall step into the box and offer an explanation when no case has been made out against him. I say that is a violation of criminal law procedure in this country.
I invite the minister to carefully read subsection 3. I think the point I make has some valid ground, and I support the submission made by the hon. member for Essex East. This is the only point I want to make. Let us not change the criminal procedure in this country by enacting a provision in this bill that the accused shall be compelled to offer an explanation before the crown has made out a case. The accused is not now obliged to do so until a case has been made out against him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a great deal of importance and, in my view, a disproportionate amount of importance has been attached to the statement made by my hon. friends that this section contravenes the bill of rights, and that what we are doing here is to provide, in effect, that the accused will be presumed guilty even in advance of the proof of the case by the crown. In other words, my hon. friends are suggesting that the mere fact that a charge is laid puts the accused on his defence and that he then has to establish his innocence. Nothing, of course could be further from the truth.
The crown, under section 33 of the new act, if this bill passes, will have to prove the facts upon which it relies to establish

the guilt of the accused. It is not until the crown has proven its case that the accused is under any obligation to enter a defence. It is a well understood principle of criminal justice that criminal statutes themselves may provide that certain inferences will be drawn from certain facts; that is all that is being done here. In every one of these cases, just as here, the crown has to establish the facts from which the statute then says that the inferences may be drawn. This is particularly true in the case of dangerous substances such as explosives, for instance, and narcotics, and now we are adding goof balls or barbiturates and amphetamines. As I say, in the case of these dangerous substances, it is common to provide that possession, in the absence of a reasonable explanation, will raise these inferences or presumptions on the basis of which the guilt of the accused can then be assumed if the accused is not able to make a reasonable explanation of the origin and purpose of his possession of these dangerous substances. This is a well understood principle of criminal law.
There is another well understood principle of criminal law, and it is this. When you are dealing with the necessity of proving your case, there is a point at which it is proper that the onus of rebuttal should pass to the accused. This again is particularly the situation with regard to those cases hinging on possession. It is, therefore, understood and accepted, and not a contravention of the bill of rights, that when the crown proves possession then the onus shifts to the accused to establish that his possession is innocent, to establish how he came into possession and the purpose for which he has possession. How could the crown possibly establish all these facts which are peculiarly and exclusively in the knowledge of the accused? He alone knows how he came into possession. He alone knows the purpose for which he possesses. It is, therefore, a well understood principle of criminal law that once the crown has proven, with respect to this category of subjects, that the accused is in possession, then the onus passes to the accused to establish that his possession is innocent and that the purpose for which he possesses is lawful.
Now, the hon. member for Essex East, particularly, has made a gross confusion of these two questions, on the one hand of the presumption of innocence and on the other hand of the transference of the onus of proof. It is because he has made this gross, selfdeceiving confusion that he has so long detained this committee in his self-defeating attempts to establish that there is here a breach of the bill of rights. The bill of rights says that no statute of the parliament of Canada shall be so interpreted as to deprive 90205-6-375

If my hon. friend looks at the bill now before the committee, he will find there is nothing in it which presumes the accused to be guilty until the crown has proven its case in accordance with the principles I have outlined. The crown has to establish the fact of possession.

The appeal was allowed. The magistrate had held that the shifting of the onus of proof provided by section 80 of the Criminal Code was abrogated by section 2 of the bill of rights, and the court of appeal of Ontario held that this was not the case.
The chief justice of the Ontario court of appeal, commenting on the argument by counsel for the accused that section 80, by putting the proof of lawful excuse upon the accused abrogates or infringes the right of the accused to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law, had the following to say:
I do not agree with this contention. Under section 80 the accused is not deprived of the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law. The law, it is true, stipulates that upon proof that accused has the explosive substance in his possession, he shall be liable to conviction unless his possession can be justified by lawful excuse. Nevertheless, it is only after conclusion of the evidence, if any, for the defence as well as the evidence for the crown that the trial tribunal is in a position to find his guilt or innocence. The presumption of innocence remains until the whole evidence is before the court. If the accused elects to adduce no evidence or if the evidence he adduces fails to support the defence of lawful excuse, then in either case he may be convicted according to law.
For these reasons, I am of the opinion that section 80 does not abrogate or infringe upon the right to be presumed innocent recognized and declared by section 2 (f) of the bill of rights.
In my submission, Mr. Chairman, this case is completely conclusive of the issue which has been raised by my hon. friends opposite, because of the words of Chief Justice Porter, applying them now to the section before this committee:
If the accused elects to adduce no evidence or the evidence he adduces fails to support the defence of lawful excuse,-
Transposing the words "fails to support the defence of lawful possession" or "innocent possession", in either case he may be convicted according to law. Just as in the case of explosives covered in section 80, the crown has to prove the fact of possession and then the onus passes to the accused to establish that the possession was lawful.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Now, sir, having disposed of the tactics of the hon. gentleman, let me deal with the only argument he really brought to buttress his position tonight and that was that by this section the accused, by virtue of the charge, is placed immediately in the position where he has to go into the box and prove his possession was innocent. Sir, this argument coming from a lawyer surprises me.
I support the claim.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Will you permit a remark at this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

The charge is possession for the purpose of trafficking. The minister will admit that. It is not just possession. The charge against the accused is possession for the purpose of trafficking. I admit that the only issue at the trial as far as the burden of the crown is concerned is possession, but

the minister must keep in mind that the charge is possession for the purpose of trafficking.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I admit that and I will deal with it, but at the moment I was dealing with the contention of the hon. member for Essex East that the moment a charge is laid the accused, if he does not plead guilty, has to go into the witness box and refute the charge of possession.
Otherwise he is found guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He does not. The onus does not lie on the accused until the crown has proven the fact on which it relies to support the charge and the fact is the fact of possession.
Possession for trafficking, not simple possession.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The charge is a charge of possession for trafficking, yes, but the fact which has to be proven, the onus of proof which lies upon the crown, is the fact of possession. It is true that the law then says that if the crown proves possession certain inferences will be drawn and then the onus is shifted to the accused of rebutting those inferences. This is a perfectly normal and proper principle of criminal justice and has been for generations. It is one of those principles which is in line with the bill of rights and was in mind when the bill of rights was drafted.
There was no bill of rights then. That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The bill of rights simply says that an accused will not be deprived of his right to be presumed innocent until he is proven guilty. The bill of rights does not say that statutes may not suggest that reasonable inferences may be drawn from certain facts so long as the onus of proving those facts is not removed from the crown. This statute says that from the fact of possession an inference may be drawn that the possession was for the purpose of trafficking and that that inference will stand unless the accused then proves that the possession was not for the purpose of trafficking. This is a perfectly proper principle of criminal justice not in the least inconsistent with the bill of rights which merely says that an accused shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty.
Once again, may I suggest in all seriousness to my hon. friends that their difficulty is that they are confusing two principles, one, onus of proof, and the other, presumption of innocence. In every criminal case the onus of proving the facts upon which the crown relies in support of its allegations lies 90205-6-376
Food and Drugs Act
on the crown. Once the crown has done that, the onus always shifts to the accused to answer the case which had been brought against him. All that you have here is a variation provided by statute as to the time at which that onus of proof shall shift, but it does not relieve the crown of the onus of proving the facts on which the crown relies to prove the allegation it has made against the accused. Yet the hon. member for Essex East solemnly said a moment or two ago that all the crown would have to do would be to lay a charge and then the accused would have to go in the witness box to prove his innocence. This is completely incorrect.
I have read subsection 1 and the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont has agreed, even if the member for Essex East has not, that the crown will have to prove the fact of possession because subsection 2 says:
If, pursuant to subsection 1, the court finds that the accused was not in possession of a controlled drug, he shall be acquitted, but, if the court finds that the accused was in possession of a controlled drug, he shall be given an opportunity of establishing-
One or the other of two things. How could the court find that he was in possession of a controlled drug unless the crown proved that he was in possession of a controlled drug?
Under this bill the proof must rest on the accused.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Read the subsection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can only say that there is a complete and deliberate refusal to understand the ordinary meaning of words.

My hon. friend
says "deliberate". Look at the words in subsection 2:
If, pursuant to subsection 1, the court finds that the accused was not in possession of a controlled drug, he shall be acquitted-
Does that support what my hon. friend has said?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Most certainly it does because how on earth does the hon. member suppose the court will find these things unless someone proves them? The subsection does not interfere with the ordinary principles of criminal justice which say that the crown shall prove its allegations. The crown is alleging possession; therefore the crown must prove possession. If the crown does not prove possession, the court cannot find possession because up to this point there is nothing for the accused to answer. It is only if the court finds possession that the accused has to answer anything, and until there is something

Food and Drugs Act
for the accused to answer he does not have to go in the box. Therefore the only way the court can find possession is if the crown proves it.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but if my hon. friend will not accept that simple point then there is probably not much use in our continuing this discussion. I can only assure him with the sincerity at my command that every lawyer he might care to consult on this matter who would consider it carefully would agree that what I have stated is correct, that the crown must prove possession before there is anything for the accused to answer. It is only then that the onus shifts to the accused and then, in accordance with proper principles of criminal justice, it is up to the accused to satisfy the court whether or not his possession was lawful or was for an innocent purpose.
It is, as I have said, an accepted practice or principle not in violation of the bill of rights that those facts which are peculiarly and exclusively within the knowledge of the accused and upon which he relies to establish his defence must be proven by the accused because, of course, it would be impossible for the crown to prove how the accused came into possession or what his state of mind was or for what purpose he acquired the drugs. That onus is on the accused to satisfy the court that his possession was lawful or was for an innocent purpose.
I suppose-in fact, I know-that we could go on and on discussing this subject but I imagine my hon. friend has now had a chance to study the case of Regina v. Guertin and the authoritative statement of the chief justice of Ontario that a section of the Criminal Code, parallel in its import and almost identical in its provisions with the section now under discussion, was not in contravention of the bill of rights. I assure the hon. member for Essex East, the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont and this committee that when we drafted the bill we did so with the greatest care because we recognized that these situations where we are trying to deal with the possession of harmful and deleterious substances do pose special problems and that one must be very careful not to go so far in one's desire to establish effective measures of control as to transgress the bill of rights. It was with that caution in our minds that we drafted this provision and it is for the reasons I have attempted to indicate to the committee that we ourselves are satisfied there is no contravention.
One final word, Mr. Chairman, and it is this. I have maintained throughout, contrary to the urgings of some of my hon. friends opposite, that the courts will, of course, have the final determination of these matters. The

courts may not agree with me. It may be that a court or, indeed the highest court, would say that they find this not to be consistent with the bill of rights. If that should be the case, then of course I would accept the verdict of the court because I respect the court. The courts are the final arbiters, the final protectors of the rights and liberties of the subject. When we introduced the bill of rights, we were at pains to explain that the courts were the final protectors because they are the final interpreters of the law. If the court does not agree with me, then I shall admit that in giving a legal opinion or a legal interpretation of this section, I was wrong. Up to this moment, and at this moment, on the basis of that clear decision of Chief Justice Porter and the other two judges of the Ontario court of appeal, reinforcing the research, the study and the consideration that we have given to it, I have no hesitation in saying that there is no contravention of the bill of rights in section 33 of the proposed Food and Drugs Act.

I do not propose to repeat my arguments, except to say that the Minister of Justice has sent me over a copy of the judgment which I have read. I would simply point out that this case undoubtedly goes a long way in support of the contention the minister has advanced. We are not advised yet as to whether or not an appeal is being lodged from the judgment of Porter, C.J.A. In any event, while this case does go a long way it is distinguishable from the section under discussion because of the wording, as I have said a number of times, of subsection 1.
I am sure that counsel arguing for the accused, confronted with this case, would point out that the language of section 33, in seeing that there is an issue tried on the question of possession, differentiates that case from this one. I cannot, however, say any more to persuade the minister. This is my honest view. A number of us here have been looking at this case, and that is our considered opinion of the difference between the Guertin case and a hypothetical case that might arise under section 33.
Finally, the minister has said that he has given his best judgment and care to the draftsmanship of this section. No one has suggested otherwise, but that does not preclude an hon. member of this house from saying that the section, as drafted, could be regarded by some hon. members as being contrary to the bill of rights. The minister has said he is going to leave to the courts the decision as to whether or not an argument of this kind is valid. Undoubtedly, the courts are going to be making decisions that will bring about many refinements in existing statutes and existing cases. The point is that we are the parliament of Canada. We are now in the process of legislating and it is our duty, in so far as we humanly can, to provide formulae to meet objections we have in mind and take steps to make corrections at this stage when enactments are in the process of being created.

I listened very carefully to the legal dissertation of the hon. member for Essex East. I hesitate to rise in the presence of such eminent counsel. Although I listened very carefully, he did not explain his inconsistency, or at least I have not been able to hear any such explanation.

The hon. member contended that the existence of the provisions in the Criminal Code and narcotics act which shifted the onus of proof to the accused, were irrelevant to this legislation because the Criminal Code and narcotics act antedated the bill of rights. Then, he went on and said that the bill of rights had no effect in changing the common law in this respect. There is an inconsistency in these two contentions which the hon. member promised to explain. I am still waiting for an explanation. If none is forthcoming or he is not capable of making an explanation, I am quite prepared to let the subject drop.

May I make one brief comment to try to satisfy the hon. member for Essex East as to the state of the law. May I assure the committee through you, sir, that we have in this case to which the Minister of Justice has referred, an authoritative decision on a set of facts which are on all fours with the type of situation which would arise under section 33. Until the Supreme Court of Canada has ruled otherwise, the finding of the supreme court of Ontario in the case of Regina v. Guertin will be binding in the province of Ontario in any prosecution which may be launched in connection with sections 33 and 34 of this act. It would have an equally binding effect, may I assure the committee, in the other provinces and would almost certainly be accepted by those courts as representing the state of the law.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the minister's remarks with great interest. I should like to examine with him a difficult case that may arise under section 33. Let us suppose a man is charged with possession of goof balls for the purpose of trafficking. Now, under section 33 (1) the crown establishes possession of these goof balls. Suppose that the accused rests on this evidence. He does not testify. The minister will admit that at this moment there is absolutely nothing illegal before the court because possession, of itself, is not illegal. Section 33 (3) provides that the accused shall be convicted if he fails to establish those matters which are contained in paragraphs (a) and (b).
I should like to come to the point where we can see whether we are wrong or whether the minister is wrong. A man is charged with possession for the purpose of trafficking. The crown establishes by evidence the fact of possession. The accused, of course, is free to enter the witness box or rest on the evidence of the crown. There is nothing in our law which forces the accused to go into the witness box.
If the accused rests on the evidence of the crown, am I right in assuming that under

Food and Drugs Act
section 33 (3) he shall be convicted of trafficking although the only fact before the court is the possession, which in itself is not an offence? I should like the minister to comment on this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would say that on the bald facts as suggested by the hon. member, that there was a charge of possession for trafficking and the crown proved possession to the satisfaction of the court-that is, they proved possession beyond a reasonable doubt-and the accused rested there and gave no answer either himself or through other witnesses, he would be convicted.
However, I think the point my hon. friend overlooks is that although the accused is convicted of possession for trafficking, he is convicted because the statute says that when the crown proves possession it is a legal, logical and proper inference to make that he was in possession for the purpose of trafficking, unless he establishes that he was not in possession for the purpose of trafficking. In other words, the statute makes that inference.
I think it might perhaps be appropriate to refer my hon. friend to one or two United States authorities where this point has been discussed. The Corpus Juris deals with this point as follows:
A statute providing that proof of one fact shall constitute prima facie evidence of the existence of another fact essential to the guilt of the accused is not void for want of due process of law, where there is some natural and rational relation or connection between the fact proved and the ultimate fact presumed and the accused is afforded a fair and reasonable opportunity to repel the presumption and submit all the facts being on the issue to the jury ...
Here you have exactly that situation. You have the fact-possession. You have the statute drawing from the fact of possession the inference that the possession was for the purpose of trafficking; and you have here some natural and rational relation or connection between the fact proved, that is the possession, and the ultimate fact presumed, that is the purpose of trafficking.
You go on and you have also the situation where the accused is afforded, and he is expressly afforded it by this statute, a fair and reasonable opportunity to repel the presumption and to submit all the facts bearing on the issue to the jury. That is the authority of Corpus Juris, and there have been a number of such cases in the United States.
There is a decision of the United States supreme court in the case of Mobile Jackson and Kansas City Railroad Company v. J. A. Turnipseed. The judgment in that case contains the following passage:
The statute does not, therefore, deny the equal protection of the law, or otherwise fail in due process of law, because it creates a presumption of
[Mr. Deschatelets.l
liability, since its operation is only to supply an inference of liability in the absence of other evidence contradicting such inference.
The judgment continues:
That a legislative presumption of one fact from evidence of another may not constitute a denial of due process of law or a denial of the equal protection of the law, it is only essential that there shall be some rational connection between the fact proved and the ultimate fact presumed, and that the inference of one fact from proof of another shall not be so unreasonable as to be a purely arbitrary mandate.
A criminal case in point where another United States supreme court decision was made is the case of Yee Hem v. United States of America, where the judge referred expressly to the presumption of innocence and the rule against self-incrimination. He said as follows:
The legislative provisions here assailed satisfy these requirements in respect of due process. They have been upheld against similar attacks, without exception so far as we are advised, by the lower federal courts.
Then the judge said:
Every accused person, of course, enters upon his trial clothed with the presumption of innocence, But that presumption may be overcome, not only by direct proof, but, in many cases, when the facts standing alone are not enough, by the additional weight of a countervailing legislative presumption. If the effect of the legislative act is to give to the facts from which the presumption is drawn an artificial value to some extent, it is no more than happens in respect of a great variety of presumptions not resting upon statute.
He went on:
The point that the practical effect of the statute creating the presumption is to compel the accused person to be a witness against himself may be put aside with slight discussion. The statute compels nothing. It does no more than to make possession of the prohibited article prima facie evidence of guilt. It leaves the accused entirely free to testify or not, as he chooses. If the accused happens to be the only repository of the facts necessary to negative the presumption arising from his possession, that is a misfortune which the statute under review does not create, but which is inherent in the case. The same situation might present itself if there were no statutory presumption, and a prima facie case of concealment with knowledge of unlawful importation were made by the evidence. The necessity of an explanation by the accused would be quite as compelling in that case as in this; but the constraint upon him to give testimony would arise there, as it arises here, simply from the force of circumstances, and not from any form of compulsion forbidden by the constitution.
I put these additional authorities from the United States on the record, Mr. Chairman, not for a moment suggesting that United States authorities are binding in Canada. I have frequently made it clear in the past that they are not. I simply put them on record because they are illustrative of the process of thought of eminent jurists who have held that provisions similar to the one now before us do not constitute an abuse of due process,

nor do they run contrary to the principle of the presumption of innocence until proven guilty.
I suggest that these United States authorities are of illustrative value only, but when they are added to an authority of binding value such as a decision of the Ontario appeal court, I hope that temporarily, at any rate, the concern and the doubts of my hon. friends will be set at rest.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is no doubt correct when he speaks about possession. Under certain conditions possession creates a presumption under the provisions of the Criminal Code. I refer to recent possession, possession of burglary tools, the possession of narcotics or the possession of explosives, where there is nothing else said as to the type of possession. Simple possession might create a presumption in those circumstances.
However, in this bill there is a qualification of the type of possession which creates the offence. Before we began discussing section 33 I bring to the minister's attention the fact that section 32 does qualify the type of possession which creates an offence under this bill.
Section 32 (2) says:
No person shall have in his possession any controlled drug for the purpose of trafficking.
So we have in this section a qualification of the type of possession which creates an offence. If we then turn to section 33 which deals with the possession, surely the minister does not think he can, under that section, sheer away from the quality of the type of possession set up in the preceding section. You cannot eliminate the type of possession you define elsewhere. You cannot read section 33 as defining possession without considering the definition created in section 32. You have established that it must be for trafficking, and when a complaint is lodged it cannot be lodged in respect of anything else. If you can prove the man was in possession for the purpose of trafficking he must explain the kind of trafficking. The moment you say nothing and remain mute with regard to the quality of possession and do not show that the accused was found in possession for trafficking, I imagine a competent defence lawyer would simply say: you have not proven the principal ingredient of the offence, namely that the accused was in possession for the purpose of trafficking.
I submit it would not stand up if the minister were to contend that an accused person was found in mere possession. You cannot say, under section 33, that mere possession means anything unless you attach to it the quality of the type of possession created
Food and Drugs Act
in the same statute in the preceding section. Once you have established the quality of the type of possession and proved that the accused has placed upon him the obligation to get into the box and defend himself or explain the circumstances of possession. But until such time as that is proven, no valid case exists. Until the crown has proved possession for the purpose of trafficking, I submit there is no burden of proof shifted to the accused. To say that mere possession of a controlled drug applies in the same way as it does with respect to a section in the Criminal Code is, in my view, altogether wrong. It is my considered opinion that section 33 when it speaks of possession means possession for the purpose of trafficking and not just simple possession.

Would the hon. member permit a question? He says that under section 31 (b) possession is defined as possession within the terms of the Criminal Code. In the Criminal Code it says:
For the purposes of this act,
(a)	a person has anything in possession when he has it in his personal possession or knowingly
(i)	has it in the actual possession or custody of another person, or
(ii)	has it in any place, whether or not that place belongs to or is occupied by him, for the use or benefit of himself or of another person; and
(b)	where one of two or more persons, with the knowledge and consent of the rest, has anything in his custody or possession, it shall be deemed to be in the custody and possession of each and all of them.
Does the hon. member not feel that this particular definition shifts the statutory onus on to the accused to prove a prima facie case that he was not in possession for the purpose of trafficking?

I shall be glad to answer that question. Of course, the definition of possession here is perfect but that applies only to the case of a definition which is not otherwise qualified by a statute. In this bill we have the word "possession" qualified and given a meaning according to all the circumstances. It does not fall within the general definition of "possession" which we have here in section 32. I shall read it once more for the benefit of the hon. member:
(1)	No person shall traffic In a controlled drug or any substance represented or held out by him to be a controlled drug.
(2)	No person shall have in his possession any controlled drug for the purpose of trafficking.
We have given meaning, here, to the type of possession intended.
