speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
I should like to say just a few words to refute the argument which the hon. member for Cartier has submitted and which the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont mentioned previously.

Food and Drugs Act
The hon. member claims that there is nothing in common between section 33 of the bill which we are considering now and the provisions of the Criminal Code under which the onus of proof rests with the accused after the crown has proved an essential fact like possession. He said that under this section, the crown merely has to prove possession, without regard to the type of possession, and that the accused has placed upon him then the obligation to explain the circumstances of possession.
There are several sections of the Criminal Code where that principle applies but I will read only the following, which is section 80:
Every one who without lawful excuse, the proof of which lies upon him,
(a) makes or has in his possession... is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years.
Now, possession in this case is qualified in that it must be without lawful excuse.
On the other hand, section 32 provides that the controlled drug in the possession of the accused must be for the purpose of trafficking; that is how possession is qualified.
In that case qualified possession must be without lawful excuse and for the purposes of trafficking.
Section 80 states that it is the accused who must prove lawful excuse. Here is what it says:
Every one who without lawful excuse, the proof of which lies upon him-
Therefore, if the accused takes the attitude that he has nothing to answer and if the crown proves possession, the court is fully justified to infer that such possession is "without lawful excuse" and, therefore, the accused may be found guilty.
Under this bill, if the accused does not submit any plea after the crown has proved possession, the crown can infer that the accused is guilty.
Therefore, there is a striking analogy between the two provisions, and in either case, the principle remains that the onus always rests with the crown to prove the accused guilty beyond any doubt; but at a certain stage of the procedure, the onus may be transferred from the crown to the accused, and even when the accused has given some proof of legal possession or has proved that he had no intention of trafficking, there again the crown may, by way of rebuttal, prove that the facts the accused attempted to establish are unfounded.
It is precisely on that point that the Ontario court of appeal gave a decision recently in

the case mentioned by the Minister of Justice: Regina v. Guertin.
Another point I should like to make in reply to the suggestion of the hon. member for Cartier, is that the accused does not necessarily have to appear in the witness box. He is free to do so if he wishes to prove his innocence or to establish that the possession of drug was not illegal. But he has many other ways of proving this and, therefore, there is no violation of the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Would the hon. member allow me a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Yes.

Suppose a person is
charged with trafficking in controlled drugs- in this case goof balls-and the crown establishes possession under section 33, but the accused decides not to move and just to adopt a waiting attitude. Would the hon. member, who has been a crown attorney, kindly tell me whether in such a case he thinks the accused should be found guilty under section 33 (3)?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not want to deal with this at great length. The accused is then in the same position as one charged under section 80 when the crown has proved possession of explosives.

Let me add only a word. Would the hon. member for Pontiac, who has acted as a crown attorney, be satisfied if one of his clients, having been brought to court under a charge of goof ball trafficking, decided not to put up any defence, and if the judge, after the crown had proved possession, found him guilty under section 33(3) of trafficking in goof balls when in fact only possession of goof balls would have been established and when possession is not an offence under the act?
Would the hon. member tell me how he can reconcile this nonsense which is something totally new in our legislation?
The minister referred a moment ago to court decisions. Never has a law with such a nonsensical provision been passed. I have never seen any, nor have I ever heard of such a thing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
It is because you do not understand.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could be allowed to reply to the hon. gentleman. He has made a fundamental error in his

judgment regarding what an accused would be convicted of. He said a moment ago that if the crown proved possession, and the accused person gave no evidence, nor took the box himself to give evidence on his own behalf, the judge would have to convict the accused of trafficking.
Yes, of trafficking.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is where my hon. friend is in error.
That is the charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read the bill he will find that the charge is possession for the purpose of trafficking. Therefore, an accused will not be convicted of trafficking, but will be convicted of having possession for the purpose of trafficking, which is very different indeed from being convicted of having trafficked or of trafficking.
Would the hon. minister answer a question at this point? How will an accused be found guilty of an offence which has not been proven?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The offence must be proven by evidence presented in conjunction with the inference of fact which the statute creates. The statute creates an inference of fact. That is, once it has been proven that an accused was in possession of goof balls, the statute creates the inference that the possession was for the purpose of trafficking, and the onus shifts to the accused to establish that the possession was lawful or was not for that purpose.
Would the minister say that an accused would be found guilty because the accused remained silent?
That is the whole point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The accused is always found guilty if he remains silent after the crown has proven a prima facie case.
Does the minister contend that when the crown has proven simple possession, without establishing that the possession was for the purpose of trafficking, that would be a prima facie case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Oh, most certainly, in the light of the inference which the statute creates, as other statutes in many cases create inferences. For example, section 80 of the Criminal Code creates the inference that possession is for an unlawful purpose. In that case the crown does not have to prove the unlawful purpose, but merely the possession. Once that has been established the section provides that the onus is upon the accused to prove lawful possession. The supreme court of Ontario has held that
Food and Drugs Act
there is no contravention of the bill of rights in this regard. This statute creates the inference that an accused, who has been found to be in possession, is in possession for the purpose of trafficking, and the onus then falls upon him to prove otherwise.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has sought vainly to impress us with the validity of his position. We in turn have sought vainly to give him the facts as to the interpretation of this bill, as we see them in the light of this section. I suggest to the minister that we have now reached the point where we cannot convince one another. The fact is that throughout this discussion there has existed an honest difference of opinion. However, that difference of opinion, I suggest, is strongly indicative of that which will happen in the case of any statute which we believe to have been formulated ambiguously without the kind of precision which should obtain, having in mind the objective.
The minister has rejected our interpretation, and has refused to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont, that this matter be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada for an opinion which could be readily obtained before the end of June, thereby clearly establishing the situation, giving to this act the effect of the purpose intended. We cannot do any more than we have done. We believe that our position is sound. We believe the Guertin case, while similar in one particular, is distinguishable in another.
For these reasons we believe that section 2 of the bill of rights will be violated by this proposed act, in that the presumption of innocence principle has not been recognized. We believe that the Minister of Justice in consequence has failed to act in accordance with section 3 of the bill of rights, which causes him to advise this house in respect of any draft or bill which is in violation of the bill of rights, or which could be regarded as a violation or contravention of that statute. We have had a long argument this afternoon, during which we have presented our opinions. We regret that we are unable to convince the Minister of Justice. Nevertheless, we are certain that this legislation will be contested in the courts by defence counsel in the way that we have indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to admit that the legislation will be tested in the courts. I am also prepared to admit that there is a difference of opinion here. There was a difference of opinioii between counsel in the Guertin case. That difference of opinion was so strong that counsel felt it was worth while to appeal the decision. My point is, that

Food and Drugs Act
counsel on one side was satisfied there was no violation of the bill of rights, and that point of view was upheld in the courts. The situation is similar here. We are satisfied that the hon. gentlemen have argued their case with just as much vehemence as persuasive force, but they have not convinced me that they are right. If the courts agree with my hon. friend, then I shall be the first to admit that he was right.
Will the minister permit a question at this time? He spoke about the Guertin case. Is this the case where explosives were involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Under section 80 of the code?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Mr. Chairman, the thing that has concerned me particularly is the reasoning of the hon. member for Essex East. On the one hand, he says that the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean has done a tremendous service to the nation in publicizing the goof ball problem. The hon. member for Ou-tremont-St. Jean has in effect indicated the tremendous danger of those goof balls and the fact that they can be put into soft drinks and alcohol. In fact, they are almost like handling dynamite. When by this legislation the crown has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that somebody has in his possession what is clearly in effect dynamite ready to blow up, then it seems reasonable that the person who has it in his possession is the person who would himself know why he has it in his possession and should be called on to give a reasonable explanation why he has it in his possession. Under the legislation he does not have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt why he has this dynamite. As I see it, he merely has to give a reasonable explanation. He can give any explanation, such as that he obtained it from a druggist, or by prescription, or any other explanation which is inconsistent with trafficking.
But the hon. member for Essex East says, on the one hand, I am trying to back up my hon. friend from Outremont-St. Jean but on the other hand I do not understand what is going on. He wants to set loose this dynamite-
We want a good bill.

-which is doing damage to a great number of juveniles whom the federal government has sought to protect by bringing in this legislation. The persons that we are trying to protect are those who, if they have goof balls in their possession, are quite competent to give a very reasonable and

innocent explanation of their possession. I think the legislation is quite clear. The legislation when enacted will enact what we have had in legislation in many years past and what they have in legislation in the United Kingdom as well.
I am shocked and amazed at my hon. friend from Essex East taking this very negative view of this excellent legislation which his hon. friend from Outremont-St. Jean has backed up. I just cannot understand it.

I had not intended to say any more on this bill, but the remarks of my hon. friend cause me to say this. We believe this bill is needed. The other night when this matter was discussed we indicated our support of the principle of the bill and we also indicated we believed that it was as a result of the efforts of the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean that the government had been persuaded at long last to bring forward this legislation. Are we to take the position, which the hon. gentleman seeks to place us in, that because we support this bill and because at the same time we find that in our judgment one of its provisions violates the bill of rights we are not to point it out? That is the argument of my hon. friend. That is what my hon. friend is now indicating. By his remarks he wants to leave the impression that although we have praised the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean, although we have praised this bill, we are now in effect taking a position which suggests that this bill should not be passed in this form and consequently the corrective measures envisaged should not be pursued.
We want this bill to operate; we want it to operate in a most effective way. It is not characteristic of the hon. gentleman, for whom I have the highest esteem, to say that because we point out what we believe to be a violation of one section of the bill of rights, on that account we are to be justifiably accused of not being in favour of so positive a measure as this. That was not worthy of the hon. gentleman. There is no consistency whatsoever.
I should have thought that the hon. member who was so enthused over the Prime Minister's championing of the bill of rights would be the first to join with us in pointing out to the Minister of Justice that he as one of the precursors of this bill of rights has now been proven to be one of its most serious violators. That is what I thought the hon. gentleman would do. Instead of that he seeks to suggest that we are not in favour of this constructive measure.

I can come to no other conclusion.

Food and Drugs Act
Everyone in this chamber is in favour of this bill and we can thank the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean for it.

A little while ago I asked the minister a question with relation to the Guertin case, which he cited. I wish to refer to the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscam-ingue who also spoke on section 80 of the Criminal Code. I see a difference between the clause we are considering and section 80 of the Criminal Code. Let me read section 80:
Every one who without lawful excuse, the proof of which lies upon him,
(b) has in his possession a bomb, grenade or other explosive weapon,
is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable-
And so forth.
If I were wording the section I would say:
Every one who has in his possession a bomb, grenade, or other explosive weapon is guilty of an indictable offence except that he may have a lawful excuse, the proof of which lies upon him.
The first principle of section 80 of the Criminal Code is that possession of an explosive is an unlawful act. Then, when the crown has proven that, the accused may bring forward an excuse. The Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, chapter 201 of the statutes of 1952, section 4, provides that the mere possession is an offence. In the bill that we shall be discussing later, namely Bill No. C-100, mere possession is an offence. In this instance mere possession is not an offence and, therefore, it is my view that the crown should be obliged to discharge the complete onus of proving that possession is for the purpose of trafficking, and not just mere possession.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I have a concrete example to give. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) told us the other day that he could not in the circumstances, and we understand him, make an offence of a simple possession because each of us has at home some of those barbiturates when they are needed.
Well, according to clause 33 of the bill before us, related to clause 36, any law officer may come to my house, take away the barbiturates which I may have in my medicine cabinet and bring me to court for possession and for traffic of barbiturates. Then, I have to prove that lawfully bought those barbiturates at a drug store and that I am entitled to have them.
I therefore submit that clause 33 goes really too far and I again urge the minister to consider our views.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to prolong this discussion. I would simply refer my hon. friend from Megantic to the fact that if he will read section 80 of the Criminal Code, which was the section in question in the Guertin case, he will surely agree with me that it is not the simple fact of possession which is the offence; it is possession without lawful excuse, and the onus of proving lawful excuse is, by the section, placed explicitly on the accused.
Here the charge is possession for the purpose of trafficking. The crown has to prove possession, then the onus is on the accused to prove the possession was lawful or was not for the purpose of trafficking. The situation seems to me very closely paralleled. May I just remind my hon. friend that all the accused has to prove to rebut the presumption which proof of possession has raised is either that he acquired the material from a druggist through a prescription, that he got it through a prescription, or that he does not have it for the purpose of trafficking. As I say, he can rebut the presumption by proving either that his possession was innocent or that it was not for an unlawful purpose. I cannot go further than that. The two cases do seem to me to be very much on all fours.

Would the minister permit a further question? Does he not agree that under section 80 possession is presumed first to be unlawful and then it is up to the accused to prove that it was lawful for him to have the dynamite or explosive? In this case it may be lawful to have goof balls in one's possession.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot agree with that. Possession under section 80 is not presumed to be unlawful because the section says "Every one who without lawful excuse". Therefore it is recognized that possession may be lawful. It is recognized by section 80 that possession may be lawful but the onus is on the accused to prove a lawful excuse. So here by section 33 it is recognized that possession may be for an innocent purpose but it is up to the accused to prove either that possession was innocent or that it was for an innocent purpose. I could not envisage anything very much more closely parallel than these two sections.

I should like to carry that point further. I have listened very carefully tonight to lawyers on both sides of the house and I must frankly admit that for most of the time they were away over my head. However, as a layman I should like to pursue this matter for a moment. The minister said that it is not presumed that people are in illegal possession of these substances but

Food and Drugs Act
in the same breath he said that all the crown has to do is to prove that they have possession and once the crown has proved that the onus is on the accused to prove that he does not have possession illegally. That is the crux of the whole thing. If the crown proves you have possession then, as I have listened to the discussion and understood it, you have possession illegally unless you can prove otherwise. I think that is the whole point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You have it for an unlawful purpose unless you prove otherwise. That is quite true. Just as in section 80, unless you prove you have it for a lawful purpose you are presumed to have it for an unlawful purpose.

I am not familiar with the sections of the bill of rights, but is this not contrary to British justice under which you are innocent until you are proven guilty? In this instance you are guilty unless you can prove yourself innocent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have endeavoured all evening to explain and to establish, and I think with success
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-that it is not contrary to the principles of criminal justice which for years have drawn a distinction between presumption of innocence and onus of proof. The crown always has the onus of proof and it is not until the crown has proven a prima facie case that the onus of replying passes to the accused. Proof of the case may be by inference from facts which the crown establishes and these inferences may be drawn either by the court itself from the circumstances or because a statute establishes that certain inferences can be drawn from these facts. That is what is done here.
If my hon. friend will look at the section, he will see that the crown has to prove possession. The onus then shifts to the accused and the accused can establish innocent possession. If he makes out a prima facie case in that regard, the onus shifts back to the crown to rebut it. There is no shifting at any time of the principle that the accused is innocent until proven guilty. It is a matter of the burden of proof.
If he does not prove innocent possession, he is automatically guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Once the crown has proven the facts upon which it relies, yes.
